issues.legal_issue: A bona fide purchaser without notice who makes improvements to mortgaged property may receive compensation for those improvements in a suit for redemption and possession.
material_facts: The purchaser acquired the property without notice of the mortgage and made improvements to it.
The suit sought redemption and possession, and the purchaser claimed compensation for the improvements.
issues.conclusion: The equitable principle in Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act applied to determine the parties’ equities, and a decree requiring compensation for the improvements as a condition of possession could be passed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act lays down an equitable principle for determining the parties’ equities. The Court relied on Narayanaswami Ayyar v. Rama Ayyar, 57 Ind. App. 305 (AIR 1930 PC 297), as supporting the application of that principle and the form of decree in a redemption and possession suit.

predicates.redemption_and_possession_proceeding: The proceeding seeks redemption of mortgaged property and possession of it.
predicates.bona_fide_purchase_without_notice: The purchaser acquired the property in good faith without notice of the mortgage.
predicates.purchaser_made_improvements: The purchaser made improvements to the property.

issues.definition: When a redemption and possession proceeding concerns a good-faith purchaser without notice who improved the property, the purchaser is entitled to equitable compensation.

issues.legal_issue: When evidence permits, the value of improvements for compensation should be assessed as near as possible to the date of actual eviction rather than the date the claimant elected to pay for them.
material_facts: The claimant elected to pay compensation and take possession before the purchaser was actually dispossessed.
The purchaser argued that compensation should reflect the value of the improvements at actual dispossession.
The Court had valuation evidence for dates nearer to actual dispossession than the date of election.
issues.conclusion: If the evidence enables the court to do so, it should assess the value of the improvements at a date as near as possible to actual eviction, rather than at the date of election.
issues.legal_principle: The Court construed Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act as an equitable principle and stated that, where evidence permits, valuation should be made as near as possible to actual eviction. The judgment cited no earlier case for this timing rule.

predicates.compensation_for_property_improvements_p: The proceeding requires the court to assess compensation for improvements made to property.
predicates.evidence_allows_later_valuation: The available evidence permits the court to assess the improvements’ value at a time near actual eviction.
predicates.election_precedes_actual_eviction: The claimant elected how to proceed before the improved property was actually taken from its possessor.

issues.definition: When compensation for property improvements is being assessed, later valuation evidence is available, and election preceded actual eviction, the improvements are valued near actual eviction.

issues.legal_issue: Compensation for improvements is measured by the value they add to the property as a saleable subject, not simply by the amount spent on them.
material_facts: The purchaser did not produce his books of account, and the evidence did not establish the exact construction costs.
A qualified court-appointed Commissioner provided valuation evidence for the old building and the new construction at different times.
The Court assessed the improvement by comparing the value of the property with the new construction against the value of the old building.
issues.conclusion: The relevant measure was the worth of the improvement in the property as a saleable subject, and the Court assessed compensation on that basis using the available valuation evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Under the equitable approach applied through Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, actual cost does not conclude the inquiry; the relevant measure is the value of the improvement in the property as a saleable subject. The Court referred to Kidar Nath v. Mathu Mal, 40 Cal. 555, in discussing the significance of producing accounts that could assist in determining the amount spent.

predicates.compensation_for_property_improvements_p: The proceeding requires the court to assess compensation for improvements made to property.
predicates.improvement_value_evidence_available: Evidence is available from which the court can assess the value added to the property by the improvements.

issues.definition: When a proceeding requires compensation for property improvements and evidence of their value is available, compensation is measured by the value they add to the property as a saleable subject.

issues.legal_issue: A dispossessed improver is entitled to restitution if the claimant fails to pay the outstanding compensation required for possession.
material_facts: The purchaser had already been dispossessed.
The Court increased the compensation payable for the improvements and credited the amount already deposited in court.
The Court directed that the purchaser would be entitled to restitution if the claimant failed to pay the remaining compensation.
issues.conclusion: The purchaser was entitled to restitution if the claimant failed to pay the balance of the compensation after crediting the amount already deposited.
issues.legal_principle: The Court ordered restitution as a consequence of non-payment of the outstanding compensation required for the claimant to obtain possession; it cited no separate provision or earlier case for this remedy.

predicates.improver_already_dispossessed: The person who made improvements has already been dispossessed of the property.
predicates.compensation_balance_remains_unpaid: The claimant has not paid the outstanding compensation required for possession.

issues.definition: If an improver has already been dispossessed and the required compensation remains unpaid, the improver is entitled to restitution.
